area.title: Address book: add and edit an address
area.scope: Adding an address to the address book (choosing a type or category, postcode or address lookup, manual entry, the fields, usages and their hints, validation, saving, the return to a journey section or contact address, today's add handshake on the INS side and the dev-only lookup spike) and editing an address (prefill, fields, validation, save and cancel); the address record, its fields and validation, and the create, read-one and update APIs and their error shapes. Stops at the list, view and delete (address-book-list).

sources.role: the owner's decisions: outranks every other source. Search boxes use the real frontend's accessible component with MDM's entries. JavaScript behaviour follows the toolbox rule with graceful degradation; JavaScript-only prototype behaviour, pop-ups included, waits on design in its own theme. Commodity catalogue and search wait on MDM; transporter management waits on requirements; the INS dashboard's summary information waits on its requirements. The overview, review, declaration and confirmation are set-owned, and shared parts change add-only. Where plants has the same page or behaviour, the same increment changes it. Each notification list is reframed in its own frontend. The report groups work as ready or blocked. Claims marked as the orchestrator's apply Sam's principles and are not his rulings; ruling:sam-2026-10-09-templates covers templates and the dashboard narrowing.

claims.statement: Sam rules that the prototype's search and autocomplete controls are not accessible and not production grade, because they are AI-generated prototype code rather than GDS components.
claims.quote: Now we need to be really careful here because the prototype isn't accessible. It's not using some GDS stuff. It's using prototype thrown up by AI stuff. ... the prototype isn't necessarily production-grade with its solution.

claims.statement: Sam rules that for a search box the precedence is not 'prototype always wins': the component used may be the one already in the real frontends, where it has been deemed accessible.
claims.quote: only use a version of auto complete or search or whatever that has been deemed accessible and meets our requirements. If it has been, the sort of precedence needs to be a little bit different than prototype always wins. In terms of the component being used, it might be the one that's actually in the frontend or frontends.

claims.statement: Sam rules that the prototype's JavaScript behaviour is not GDS compliant and is not to be blindly replicated by adding lots of JavaScript to the frontend, for accessibility and maintainability reasons.
claims.quote: the prototype is doing stuff with JavaScript that is not GDS compliant. This isn't stuff that can just be blindly replicated by chucking a tonne of JavaScript in the frontend. ... 'Do things like add all this JavaScript stuff for accessibility concerns and maintainability concerns.'

claims.statement: Sam rules that GDS components are the toolbox, and where one is not available another tested, accessible government library (such as Ministry of Justice or Scottish Government) is used.
claims.quote: We really try to strictly head here to GDS components as a toolbox, and where that's not available, use other government libraries like a Ministry of Justice or a Scottish Government component that has been tested and meets accessibility requirements.

claims.statement: Sam rules there is a graceful degradation requirement: CSS and JavaScript may enhance behaviour, but every page must work without JavaScript, so the prototype's way of doing things may not be possible or wanted in the real service.
claims.quote: We've got a graceful degradation requirement on this, like any other GDS project, which means you can use things like CSS and JavaScript to enhance behaviour, but you need graceful degradation. It needs to be able to work without JavaScript, and that means that the way things are done in the prototype may not be possible or even desired in the real thing.

claims.statement: Sam rules that, as a pre-step for these increments, three questions are answered: is it possible with off-the-shelf GDS; if not, with other complementary off-the-shelf components; if not, why is the atypical thing strongly required. At that point it goes back to design to push back.
claims.quote: Almost as a pre-step for some of these increments, we need to get answers to that stuff: - Is it possible using off-the-shelf GDS? - If it isn't, is it using available, off-the-shelf, other complementary components? - If it isn't, why is this atypical thing strongly required? At that point, we go back to design and say, 'Come on, we don't need this.'

claims.statement: A behaviour the prototype gives with JavaScript is built only if it passes these tests in order: GOV.UK Frontend's components and patterns first; then another tested government library (Ministry of Justice, HMRC, Scottish Government); otherwise it goes back to design, which must say why it is strongly needed.
claims.quote: GOV.UK Frontend's components and patterns are used first. Where they have nothing, another tested government library is used, such as the Ministry of Justice's, HMRC's or the Scottish Government's. Where neither has anything, the behaviour goes back to design, which must say why it is strongly needed.
claims.note: Marked 'Sam (point 3)'. HMRC is named in claim 5 but not in Sam's quote, which names Ministry of Justice and Scottish Government only; the examples are illustrative ('like').

sources.role: the owner's decisions, as narrowed by ruling:sam-2026-10-09: on look and feel the prototype wins by default over what the real services do today; only a DR1 judgement on the same difference, or a real constraint the prototype cannot express (persistence, validation, authentication, cross-service behaviour), overrides it. claims.quote: The DR1 parity backlog. [...] It is not a source of requirements.

claims.quote: It is not a source of requirements. Use it only when the real frontend and the prototype clash
claims.note: New. The main session's claim 3 states this in so many words; the quote implies it.

claims.statement: The DR1 parity backlog is used only where the real frontend and the prototype clash.
claims.quote: Use it only when the real frontend and the prototype clash
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Where DR1 already made a judgement on that same difference between the real frontend and the prototype, the DR1 judgement is followed.
claims.quote: if DR1 already made a judgement on that difference, follow it and cite the row.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Where a DR1 judgement is followed, the DR1 parity backlog row it comes from is cited.
claims.quote: follow it and cite the row.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The prototype (Design Release 2.1) wins by default over what the real services do today.
claims.quote: Precedence: the prototype wins by default.
claims.note: New. 'Over what the real services do today' is the main session's framing; it follows from the Goal paragraph.

claims.statement: A DR1 judgement on the same difference overrides the prototype default.
claims.quote: Only a DR1 judgement or a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. 'On the same difference' comes from the DR1 paragraph (lines 8-9).

claims.statement: A real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype default; the ruling names persistence, validation, authentication and cross-service behaviour as such constraints.
claims.quote: a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. The quote says 'auth'; claim 6 reads it as authentication. Claim 6 adds 'such as', making the list examples; the quote's parenthesis can be read either as examples or as the full list.

claims.statement: Nothing other than a DR1 judgement on the same difference or a real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype.
claims.quote: Only a DR1 judgement or a real constraint the prototype can't express (persistence, validation, auth, cross-service behaviour) overrides it.
claims.note: New. In particular, what a real service does today is not on its own a reason to depart from the prototype.

claims.statement: Questions for people are kept to a minimum.
claims.quote: Decisions: keep questions for people to a minimum.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: A question for people is raised only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the prototype default nor a DR1 judgement settles it.
claims.quote: Raise one only when a difference is truly exceptional and neither the default nor DR1 settles it.
claims.note: New. Both conditions must hold. 'The default' is read as the prototype-wins default from the Precedence paragraph.

claims.statement: Increments are grouped into themes, and the themes are drawn from the evidence.
claims.quote: Themes: group the increments into themes based on the evidence.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Each theme's boundary is set by the code it touches.
claims.quote: Draw the boundaries by the code each one touches
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: Themes can be built in parallel on separate machines without pull requests that conflict with each other.
claims.quote: so themes can be built in parallel on separate machines without conflicting PRs.
claims.note: New.

claims.statement: The ruling's DR1 paragraph has an elision marked [...]: what the omitted words said about the DR1 parity backlog is not recorded.
The ruling does not say what makes a difference 'truly exceptional', so when a question for people is warranted is left open.

The ruling limits DR1 use to clashes between 'the real frontend' and the prototype; it does not say which frontend that is, or whether DR1 judgements apply to differences in the INS frontend, the backends or other repos.
The ruling does not say which override wins when a DR1 judgement and a real constraint the prototype cannot express point different ways on the same difference.
The ruling does not say what a real service does where a real constraint overrides the prototype: whether it keeps today's behaviour or matches the prototype as closely as the constraint allows.
The ruling does not say whether a feature or behaviour a real service has that Design Release 2.1 does not show at all counts as a difference to remove, or is left alone.
The ruling does not say what to do where the code two themes need to touch overlaps, so no boundary keeps their pull requests from conflicting.

sources.role: what exists today and what has already been ruled; the real persistence, validation and authorisation constraints the prototype cannot express

claims.statement: An address-book entry is untyped and owned by an organisation: it has no type or role, and no operator-type categorisation.
claims.quote: An untyped, organisation-owned address-book entry.

claims.statement: An address is one flat set of fields (the Standard Address Block), with no nested address object.
claims.quote: The field set is flat — the Standard Address Block is one flat form, so there is no nested {@code Address} value object.

claims.statement: The stored address holds these fields: id, name, addressLine1, addressLine2, townOrCity, county, postcode, countryCode, phone, email, organisationId, status, createdAt, modifiedAt, expireAt and version.
claims.quote: private String id; private String name; private String addressLine1; private String addressLine2; private String townOrCity; private String county; private String postcode; private String countryCode; private String phone; private String email; private String organisationId; private AddressStatus status; @CreatedDate private Instant createdAt; @LastModifiedDate private Instant modifiedAt; private Instant expireAt; @Version private Long version;

claims.statement: Ruling cv-011: countryCode is stored as an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code exactly as supplied; the service never converts it to or from a country display name.
claims.quote: {@code countryCode} is stored as an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code (cv-011), exactly as supplied — the service does not convert it to or from a display name.

claims.statement: createdAt is set automatically when an address is first saved, and modifiedAt is updated automatically on every write, including an update and a soft delete.
claims.quote: {@code modifiedAt} is bumped by auditing on every write (PUT and soft delete)

claims.statement: modifiedAt is for audit only: nothing in the service reads it to drive any other behaviour.
claims.quote: but is audit only: nothing reads it to refresh anything.

claims.statement: Each stored address carries a version number used for optimistic locking, which is never returned to callers.
claims.quote: @Version private Long version;
claims.note: Optimistic locking is inferred from Spring Data's @Version annotation; the mapper ignores version when building the response. How a version conflict surfaces to a caller is not in this part.

claims.statement: The stored entity is never sent to callers directly: a separate response object defines what the API returns.
claims.quote: The entity is never serialised onto the wire — the response records own the wire contract.

claims.statement: The same request body is used both to create an address and to replace one, and its JSON field names are camelCase.
claims.quote: Create/update request body. The wire is camelCase (global {@code JacksonConfig}), so every field serialises under its Java name.

claims.statement: name is required; a blank name is rejected with the message "Enter a name".
claims.quote: @NotBlank(message = "Enter a name")

claims.statement: name may be at most 255 characters; a longer one is rejected with the message "Name must be 255 characters or less".
claims.quote: @Size(min = 1, max = 255, message = "Name must be 255 characters or less")

claims.statement: name is described as the display name for the address, with the example "Highland Livestock Ltd".
claims.quote: description = "Display name for the address", ... example = "Highland Livestock Ltd")

claims.statement: addressLine1 is required; a blank one is rejected with the message "Enter address line 1".
claims.quote: @NotBlank(message = "Enter address line 1")

claims.quote: @Size(min = 1, max = 255, message = "Address line 1 must be 255 characters or less")

claims.statement: addressLine1 is described as the first line of the postal address, with the example "14 Drover's Way".
claims.quote: description = "First line of the postal address", ... example = "14 Drover's Way")

claims.statement: addressLine2 is optional and may be at most 255 characters; a longer one is rejected with the message "Address line 2 must be 255 characters or less".

claims.note: The errors map's wire shape (the validation problem response) belongs to part 2.

claims.statement: Ruling cv-044: the address book is untyped and unroled, so a request that supplies a type gets a per-field 400 error on type with the message "type is not a supported field".
claims.quote: {@code type} and {@code role} are the one exception (cv-044): the address book is untyped and unroled ... A supplied value binds and fails {@code @Null}, landing in the same Bean-Validation {@code errors} map keyed {@code type} / {@code role} — a per-field 400, not a silent drop and not a deserialization failure. ... @Null(message = "type is not a supported field")

claims.statement: Ruling cv-044: a request that supplies a role gets a per-field 400 error on role with the message "role is not a supported field".
claims.quote: @Null(message = "role is not a supported field")

claims.statement: type and role are hidden from the published API request schema and are never saved onto the address.
claims.quote: present for Bean Validation and absent from the generated OpenAPI request schema. ... They are never mapped onto the entity.

claims.statement: Server-assigned fields supplied in a create or update body (id, organisationId, deleted, status and the timestamps) are silently ignored, not rejected: a body that echoes a previous read is accepted.
claims.quote: Server-assigned fields ({@code id}, {@code organisationId}, {@code deleted}, timestamps) are not components here, so they are ignored if supplied — Spring Boot leaves {@code fail-on-unknown-properties} off (Zalando default): a body echoing a read-only field from a prior GET is accepted and the field dropped, never a 400.

claims.statement: Any other unknown field in a create or update body is also ignored rather than rejected.
claims.quote: Spring Boot leaves {@code fail-on-unknown-properties} off
claims.note: Follows from unknown-property failure being off globally; only type and role are modelled to be rejected.

claims.statement: The service, not the caller, sets an address's id, organisationId, status and timestamps on create and update.
claims.quote: Server-owned fields ({@code id}, {@code organisationId}, {@code status}, timestamps) are set by the service on create/update, not here.

claims.statement: An update is a full replace of the client-supplied fields: an optional field (addressLine2 or county) left out of the update body is cleared on the stored address.
claims.quote: Applies a full replace of client-supplied fields onto an existing entity. ... void updateEntity_replacesAllMutableFieldsAndClearsOmittedOptionals()

claims.statement: An update keeps the address's id, organisationId, status, createdAt and version as they were.
claims.quote: assertThat(existing.getId()).isEqualTo("665f1c2ab3e4d51a2c9d0e77"); assertThat(existing.getOrganisationId()).isEqualTo("ORG-001"); assertThat(existing.getStatus()).isEqualTo(AddressStatus.ACTIVE); assertThat(existing.getCreatedAt()).isEqualTo(Instant.parse("2026-07-01T09:00:00Z"));
claims.note: The mapper test leaves modifiedAt unchanged; modifiedAt is then bumped by auditing on save (claim repo-addressbook-p1-005).

claims.statement: An address returned by the API has these fields: id, name, addressLine1, addressLine2, townOrCity, county, postcode, countryCode, phone, email, organisationId, deleted, createdAt and modifiedAt.
claims.quote: String id, ... String name, ... String addressLine1, ... String addressLine2, ... String townOrCity, ... String county, ... String postcode, ... String countryCode, ... String phone, ... String email, ... String organisationId, ... boolean deleted, ... Instant createdAt, ... Instant modifiedAt

claims.statement: Every returned field is always present except addressLine2 and county, which are optional.
claims.quote: {@code addressLine2} and {@code county} are genuinely optional and left unguarded.

claims.statement: The response never returns status, version or expireAt.
claims.quote: @BeanMapping(ignoreUnmappedSourceProperties = {"status", "version", "expireAt"})

claims.statement: Ruling cv-016: a soft-deleted address is shown to callers as a deleted boolean (true when its status is DELETED, false when ACTIVE), never as the internal status value.
claims.quote: The soft-delete tombstone is exposed as a derived {@code deleted} boolean (cv-016), never the internal status enum. ... @Mapping(target = "deleted", expression = "java(address.getStatus() == AddressStatus.DELETED)")

claims.statement: If a stored address is missing a required field, building its response fails loudly with a server error rather than returning a partial record.
claims.quote: Server-constructed and always-present fields are null-guarded in the compact constructor (service-boundary rule): a null here is a server bug and fails loud, not a malformed wire value.

claims.statement: The returned id is an opaque identifier, shown with the example "665f1c2ab3e4d51a2c9d0e77".
claims.quote: description = "Opaque address identifier", ... example = "665f1c2ab3e4d51a2c9d0e77")

claims.statement: organisationId in the response is the organisation that owns the address.
claims.quote: description = "Organisation that owns this address"

claims.quote: description = "Creation timestamp (UTC)", ... format = "date-time" ... void response_serialisesInstantFieldsAsIso8601NotEpochMillis()

claims.statement: The response is described as "An address in the caller's organisation-scoped address book", and the request as "Create or replace an address in the caller's address book".
claims.quote: @Schema(description = "An address in the caller's organisation-scoped address book") ... @Schema(description = "Create or replace an address in the caller's address book")

claims.quote: required: - addressLine1 - countryCode - email - name - phone - postcode - townOrCity

claims.statement: The published API schema does not mark email with an email format; the email format check exists only in the service's validation.
claims.quote: email: type: string description: Contact email address example: exports@highlandlivestock.example.com maxLength: 254 minLength: 1
claims.note: Inferred from the absence of `format: email` in the generated schema while AddressRequest.java:94 carries @Email.

claims.statement: An address has one of two statuses: ACTIVE or DELETED.
claims.quote: public enum AddressStatus { ACTIVE, DELETED }

claims.statement: Ruling cv-016: a DELETED address is a soft-delete tombstone; it is left out of lists but can still be read by id, so a caller can tell "deleted" (200 with deleted true) from "unknown" (404).
claims.quote: Soft-delete tombstone status (cv-016). {@code DELETED} addresses are excluded from lists but remain readable by id so a consumer can distinguish "deleted" (200 + DELETED) from "unknown" (404).

claims.statement: A soft delete keeps the record in the database, flips its status to DELETED and updates modifiedAt; only a 200 with deleted true means the user deleted the address.
claims.quote: the document stays in MongoDB, its internal `status` flips to `DELETED`, and `modifiedAt` is bumped. The tombstone remains fetchable by id with `deleted: true` on the wire. ... Only a **200** response with `deleted: true` means the user deleted this address.
claims.note: The DELETE endpoint itself, its 204 and idempotency belong to part 2.

claims.statement: In prod, addresses and their tombstones are kept indefinitely, at roughly 1 KB each.
claims.quote: In prod, addresses and tombstones are retained indefinitely (~1 KB each).

claims.statement: Addresses are stored in MongoDB, in the collection "addresses" of the database "trade-imports-address-book" (overridable with MONGO_DATABASE).
claims.quote: **Database:** `trade-imports-address-book` (override with `MONGO_DATABASE`) **Collection:** `addresses`

claims.statement: The addresses collection has one compound index, org_status_created, on organisationId ascending, status ascending and createdAt descending, which serves every production read: organisation-scoped, active only, newest first.
claims.quote: The single compound index {@code org_status_created} serves every production read: org-scoped, status-bounded (ACTIVE), newest-first. ... @CompoundIndex(name = "org_status_created", def = "{'organisationId': 1, 'status': 1, 'createdAt': -1}")

claims.statement: Indexes are created automatically at service start-up, so the org_status_created index exists from when the collection is empty.
claims.quote: auto-index-creation: true ... It is built now while the collection is empty so it is never a later migration or index build on a populated collection.

claims.statement: Address books are expected to be small (one user's book, tens to hundreds of rows), so a bounded scan is acceptable, and any further index must be justified against real collection size.
claims.quote: Datasets are one user's address book today (tens to hundreds of rows), so a bounded scan is acceptable. Reassess any future index against real collection size before adding it.

claims.statement: Mongo reads default to primaryPreferred and writes to majority write concern, both overridable by environment variable.
claims.quote: read-preference: ${MONGO_READ_PREFERENCE:primaryPreferred} write-concern: ${MONGO_WRITE_CONCERN:majority}
claims.note: MongoConfig.java's class comment says the read preference is "secondary (configurable)", while application.yml defaults it to primaryPreferred. Recorded, not reconciled.

claims.statement: The service connects to Mongo with TLS enabled, using the CDP trust store, and authenticates in CDP with AWS IAM through the connection string.

claims.statement: ADDRESS_TTL_DAYS (config key address-book.ttl.days, unset by default) sets how many days after creation an address expires; when set, each new address gets an internal expireAt that is not returned to callers.
claims.quote: | `ADDRESS_TTL_DAYS` | unset | Days after creation an address expires. When set, each new address gets an internal `expireAt` (not returned on the wire). Updates and deletes keep the original `expireAt`. Must be positive. |

claims.quote: Updates and deletes keep the original `expireAt`.

claims.statement: ADDRESS_TTL_EXPIRY_ENABLED (config key address-book.ttl.expiry.enabled, false by default) creates the address_expire_at_ttl Mongo TTL index at start-up when true, after which Mongo removes addresses, active and tombstoned alike, once their expireAt has passed.
claims.ref: src/main/resources/application.yml:33-34; address/AddressExpiryIndex.java:15-49; README.md: Address expiry (non-prod only)
claims.quote: | `ADDRESS_TTL_EXPIRY_ENABLED` | `false` | When `true`, the `address_expire_at_ttl` MongoDB TTL index is created at startup and MongoDB removes documents once `expireAt` has passed — active addresses and tombstones alike. |

claims.statement: The TTL index is on expireAt ascending and expires each address at exactly its expireAt time (zero seconds after).

claims.statement: In the running service an unset ENVIRONMENT does not stop start-up: application.yml defaults it to "local", which counts as non-prod, so expiry can apply. Only an ENVIRONMENT that is set but blank fails start-up.

claims.note: Inferred from the placeholder default plus @NotBlank on environment. AddressTtlConfigTest's missing-environment failure runs in a bare context without this default, so it does not show what the deployed service does.

claims.statement: The wrong-type parameter handler exists so that a non-numeric query or path parameter is a 400 rather than a 500: without it Spring's type-mismatch exception would reach the catch-all RuntimeException handler and return an internal error.
claims.quote:
A query/path parameter that could not be bound to its target type (e.g. a non-numeric
   * {@code page} or {@code page_size}) — 400 bad-request, NO errors map. Without this, Spring's
   * {@link MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException} would fall through to the 500 handler.
claims.note: The Javadoc still names page_size, which is not a request parameter today (page size is server-configured, cv-025); only page is.

claims.statement: A validation failure is logged as a warning with the framework exception's full message, which can include the submitted field values, so personal data from a rejected address may reach the logs.
claims.quote: log.warn("Validation error (trace: {}): {}", traceId, ex.getMessage());
claims.note: Inferred: Spring's MethodArgumentNotValidException message lists each field error with its rejected value. Recorded in general terms as a logging concern.

claims.statement: An unexpected error is logged at error level with its message and full stack trace and the trace id; every 4xx problem is logged only as a warning.
claims.quote: log.error("Unexpected error (trace: {}): {}", traceId, ex.getMessage(), ex);

claims.statement: The stub simulates the DEFRA address lookup gateway's address search at GET /simulator/address-lookup/v2.1/addresses.
claims.quote: @GetMapping("/simulator/address-lookup/v2.1/addresses")

claims.statement: The simulator stands in for the address lookup gateway that the INS backend calls, as part of the EUDPA-390 address lookup spike.
claims.quote: # EUDPA-390 address lookup spike — the three federated-credential simulators (plan Step 6).
claims.note: The caller being ins-backend is stated in the application.yml comment at line 115: "The audience ins-backend's Entra token request resolves to".

claims.statement: The search accepts two optional query parameters: postcode and find (free text).
claims.quote:
@RequestParam(required = false) String postcode,
        @RequestParam(required = false) String find

claims.statement: When both postcode and find are sent, postcode is used and find is ignored.
claims.quote: String term = postcode != null ? postcode : find;

claims.statement: A postcode and a find term are matched the same way, against the same reserved terms: the simulator deliberately does not model what find really matches (a postcode, building name or number, street or town), leaving that to the real gateway in dev.
claims.quote: Deliberately identical for both parameters. What find really matches — a postcode, a building name or number, a street, a town — is a question only the real gateway can answer, and a simulator that guessed would look like an answer. Local runs prove the plumbing carries the parameter through; dev settles the behaviour.

claims.statement: When neither postcode nor find is sent, the simulator answers 400 with a JSON body whose message is "Either postcode or find is required".
claims.quote: .body("{ \"statusCode\": 400, \"message\": \"Either postcode or find is required\" }");

claims.statement: Reserved terms are matched exactly, case and spacing included, so a postcode sent in lower case or without its space (for example sw1a 1aa or SW1A1AA) does not hit a fixture and gets the no-results answer.
claims.quote:
return switch (term) {
            case "SW1A 1AA" -> jsonOk(THREE_ADDRESSES_FIXTURE);
claims.note: Inferred from the Java string switch, which compares exactly, and the default branch returning NO_RESULTS_FIXTURE. Whether callers normalise the postcode before sending it is outside this source.

claims.statement: Searching for postcode SW1A 1AA returns 200 with a JSON body holding the three fixture addresses.
claims.quote: case "SW1A 1AA" -> jsonOk(THREE_ADDRESSES_FIXTURE);

claims.statement: Searching for postcode ZZ1 1ZZ returns 204 No Content with no body: the reserved no-results postcode.
claims.quote: case "ZZ1 1ZZ" -> ResponseEntity.noContent().build();

claims.statement: Searching for postcode QQ1 1QQ returns 400 with a JSON body whose message is "Requested postcode is not valid": the reserved invalid postcode.
claims.quote: .body("{\"statusCode\":400,\"message\":\"Requested postcode is not valid\"}");

claims.statement: Searching for postcode XX1 1XX returns 503 with a JSON body whose message is "Service Unavailable": the reserved throttled or unavailable postcode.
claims.quote: .body("{\"statusCode\":503,\"message\":\"Service Unavailable\"}");

claims.statement: Searching for postcode YY1 1YY returns 200 with an HTML body ("Bad Gateway") instead of JSON: the reserved proxy-error postcode.
claims.quote: case "YY1 1YY" -> ResponseEntity.ok().contentType(MediaType.TEXT_HTML).body("<html><body>Bad Gateway</body></html>");

claims.statement: Searching for postcode TT1 1TT waits 15 seconds, then returns 200 with the three fixture addresses: the reserved slow-response postcode.
claims.quote: Thread.sleep(15_000);

claims.statement: The free-text terms "Buckingham Palace" and "Downing Street" each return 200 with the three fixture addresses, so the find search can be demonstrated locally.
claims.quote: case "Buckingham Palace", "Downing Street" -> jsonOk(THREE_ADDRESSES_FIXTURE);

claims.quote: These are reserved terms like the postcodes above, NOT a model of what find matches — that is the question the spike exists to answer, and only the real gateway can. A search here returning results says nothing about whether the same search would return results in dev.

claims.quote:

claims.quote: Shaped like the real dev response of 2026-09-17, not like the published v2.1 specification

claims.statement: The three fixture addresses are the three ways a name lands in a result (the whole name in subBuildingName; a building number and street; a sub-building, building name and street), chosen because they make composing address line 1 awkward; the Buckingham Palace case is the one dev actually returned.
claims.quote: The three results are the three ways a name lands, which is what makes composing address line 1 awkward — the first is the Buckingham Palace case dev actually returned, where {@code subBuildingName} carries the whole name and {@code buildingName}, {@code buildingNumber} and {@code street} are all null.

claims.statement: Every search requires a bearer token: the simulator checks the authorisation scheme, the token's signature, its audience and its expiry before answering any search, the way a real resource server would.
claims.quote: Checks the bearer token the way a real resource server would — signature, audience, expiry — before serving the reserved-postcode fixtures
claims.note: Described in general terms only, as the brief requires.

claims.statement: A search with a missing or invalid bearer token is refused with 401 and the JSON body { "statusCode": 401, "message": "Unauthorized. Access token is missing or invalid." }, word for word what the real gateway returned in dev on 17 September 2026.
claims.quote: .body("{ \"statusCode\": 401, \"message\": \"Unauthorized. Access token is missing or invalid.\" }");

claims.statement: The 401 answer carries no WWW-Authenticate header, matching the real gateway.
claims.quote: The gateway sends no {@code WWW-Authenticate} header with it, and neither does this.

claims.statement: The bearer check runs before the search terms are looked at, so an unauthorised request gets 401 even when it sends no search term or a reserved term.

The audience the simulator expects is set by address-lookup-simulator.expected-audience, overridable with ADDRESS_LOOKUP_SIMULATOR_EXPECTED_AUDIENCE, and must match the INS backend's local and stack Scope value exactly, api:// prefix included.
claims.quote:
# The audience ins-backend's Entra token request resolves to once /.default is stripped — must
  # match the local/stack "Scope" value in the EUDPA-390 plan exactly, api:// prefix included.
claims.note: The default value is a placeholder identifier, not a secret, and is not repeated here.

claims.statement: The simulator, like the real gateway in dev, accepts only the api:// form of the audience and refuses a token whose audience is the bare identifier.
claims.quote:
# The real gateway policy in dev wants the api:// form and rejects the bare GUID, so this does
  # too: a simulator that accepted either would not have caught the 401 the spike hit.

claims.statement: No spec proves how the INS add page treats a handshake with a missing, wrong or expired handshake token, notification id or fulfilment id; only the journey-type guard is proven.

claims.statement: The address-book API creates a record for an organisation with POST /organisation/{organisationId}/addresses and a JSON body of name, addressLine1, townOrCity, postcode, countryCode, phone and email, answering 201 with a Location header for the new record.

claims.note: Called by the test to seed records, not by a page; it shows the system of record behind the picker.

claims.statement: An address-book record carries id, name, addressLine1, addressLine2, townOrCity, county, postcode, countryCode, phone, email, organisationId, a deleted flag, createdAt and modifiedAt.
claims.quote: {"id":"6ac683f36bdb2fc53f12860e","name":"Danish Meat Export Kolding1791394803707","addressLine1":"Havnegade 21","addressLine2":null,"townOrCity":"Copenhagen","county":null,"postcode":"1058","countryCode":"DK","phone":"01228 555 0197","email":"searchable@example.co.uk","organisationId":"5900001","deleted":false,"createdAt":"2026-10-07T17:40:03.716445678Z","modifiedAt":"2026-10-07T17:40:03.716445678Z"}

claims.statement: The address book add handshake takes four query parameters on /address-book/add: journey-type, notification-id, fulfilment-id and handshake-token.

claims.note: The handshake-token value in the trace is a test placeholder, not a credential.

claims.statement: The refusal renders the INS 404 page: heading 404, body Page not found, title Page not found | Import notification service, with the Address book navigation item active and no back link or onward link in the page body.
